source_text: Jam vero, percurrentibus nobis caussas impatientiae, caetera quoque praecepta suis locis respondebunt. Si detrimento rei familiaris animus concitatur, omni pene in loco de contemnendo saeculo, Scripturis dominicis commonetur: nec major ad pecuniae contemptum exhortatio subjacet, quam quod ipse Dominus in nullis divitiis invenitur. Semper pauperes justificat, divites praedamnat. Ita detrimentum patientiae fastidium opulentiae praeministravit, demonstrans per abjectionem divitiarum, laesuras quoque eorum computandas non esse. Quod ergo nobis appetere minime opus est quia nec Dominus appetivit, detruncatum vel etiam ademptum non aegre sustinere debemus. Cupiditatem omnium malorum radicem Spiritus Domini per Apostolum pronuntiavit. Eam non in concupiscentia alieni tantum constitutam interpretemur; nam et quod nostrum videtur, alienum est: nihil enim nostrum, quoniam Dei omnia, cujus ipsi quoque nos. Itaque si damno affecti impatienter senserimus, non de nostro amissum dolentes, affines cupiditatis deprehendemur. Alienum quaerimus, cum alienum amissum aegre sustinemus. Qui damni impatientia concitatur, terrena coelestibus anteponendo, de proximo in Deum peccat. Spiritum enim quem a Domino sumpsit, saecularis rei gratia concutit. Libenter igitur terrena amittamus, coelestia tueamur. Totum licet saeculum pereat, dum patientiam lucrifaciam. Jam qui minutum sibi aliquid aut furto, aut vi, aut etiam ignavia, non constanter sustinere constituit, nescio an facile, vel ex animo, ipse rei suae manum inferre posset in caussa eleemosynae. Quis enim ab alio secari omnino non sustinens, ipse ferrum in corpore suo ducit? Patientia in detrimentis, exercitatio est largiendi et communicandi. Non piget donare eum, qui non timent perdere. Alioquin quomodo duas habens tunicas, alteram earum nudo dabit, nisi idem sit, qui auferenti tunicam, etiam pallium offerre possit? Quomodo amicos de mammona fabricabimus nobis, si eum in tantum amaverimus, ut amissum non sufferamus? Peribimus cum perdito. Quid hic invenimus, ubi habemus amittere? Gentilium est, omnibus detrimentis impatientiam adhibere, qui rem pecuniariam fortasse animae anteponant. Nam et faciunt, cum lucri cupiditatibus quaestuosa pericula mercimoniorum in mari exercent; cum pecuniae caussa etiam in foro nihil damnationi timendum aggredi dubitant; cum denique ludo et castris sese locant, cum per viam in mores bestiarum latrocinantur. Nos vero secundum diversitatem, qua cum illis sumus, non animam pro pecunia, sed pecuniam pro anima deponere convenit, seu sponte in largiendo, seu patientes in amittendo.
pass_a_gloss: Now indeed, as we run through the causes of impatience, the other precepts also will respond in their own places. If the mind is stirred up by loss of family property, almost everywhere in the Scripture of the Lord we are warned about despising the world; nor is there a greater exhortation to contempt of money than that the Lord Himself is found in no riches. He always justifies the poor, condemns the rich. Thus, the loss of patience has provided a disdain for wealth, showing through the low value of riches that their losses also are not to be considered. Therefore, we ought not to grieve at what has been cut off or even taken away from us, since the Lord did not desire it. The Spirit of the Lord declared through the Apostle that greed is the root of all evils. We should not interpret this as established only in desire for what belongs to another; for even what seems to be ours is another's, since nothing is ours, because all things are God's, and we ourselves are His. Therefore, if we have sensed impatiently at loss, grieving at what has been lost as if it were ours, we are caught in greed. We seek what belongs to another when we grieve at the loss of what belongs to another. He who is stirred up by impatience at loss, putting earthly things before heavenly ones, sins against God and his neighbor. For he shakes the Spirit which he has received from the Lord for the sake of a worldly thing. Let us therefore willingly lose earthly things and keep heavenly ones. Let the whole world perish, as long as we gain patience. Now he who has not decided to endure steadfastly some small thing, whether by theft or by force or even by sloth, I do not know whether he can easily, or from the heart, lay his own hand on his property for the cause of almsgiving. For who, not enduring to be cut off by another at all, himself bears the sword in his own body? Patience in losses is an exercise in giving and sharing. He does not regret giving who does not fear losing. Otherwise, how will he who has two tunics give one of them to a naked person, unless he is the same one who can offer his cloak to him who takes his tunic? How will we make friends with money if we love it so much that we cannot endure its loss? We will perish with what is lost. What do we find here, where we have to lose? It is characteristic of Gentiles to exhibit impatience at all losses, who perhaps put money before the soul; for they do this when, with greedy desires for gain, they undertake dangerous mercantile risks at sea; when, for the sake of money, they do not hesitate to approach nothing in the forum that is to be feared; when finally they let themselves be hired for the game and for the camp, when they plunder on the road like beasts. But we, according to the difference by which we are distinct from them, ought not to put the soul before money, but money before the soul, either spontaneously in giving or patiently in losing.

pass_b_english: As we run through the causes of impatience, the other precepts will also fall into place. If the loss of family property stirs you up, the Lord's Scripture warns you in almost every passage to despise the world; no exhortation to scorn money carries more weight than the fact that the Lord Himself is found possessing no riches. He always justifies the poor and condemns the rich (Luke 12:33). Thus, losing patience actually teaches you to disdain wealth: by showing how worthless riches are, it proves that losing them does not count as harm. Therefore, since the Lord never desired wealth, we ought not to grieve over what has been cut off or even taken from us. The Spirit of the Lord declared through the Apostle that greed is the root of all evils. We must not limit this to desiring what belongs to another; even what seems to be ours belongs to someone else, since nothing is ours—all things are God's, and we ourselves belong to Him. So if we react impatiently to loss, grieving as if we lost our own, we are caught in greed. We are chasing what belongs to another when we grieve over losing what belongs to another. Anyone stirred up by impatience at loss, putting earthly things before heavenly ones, sins against his neighbor and against God. For he shakes the Spirit he received from the Lord for the sake of a worldly thing. Let us therefore lose earthly things willingly and keep heavenly ones. Let the whole world perish, as long as we gain patience. Now, the man who has not resolved to endure steadfastly even a small loss—whether by theft, violence, or mere neglect—I doubt he can easily, or from the heart, put his hand to his own property for the sake of almsgiving. For who, refusing to endure being cut by another, turns the sword against his own body? Patience in loss is the training ground for giving and sharing. The man who does not fear losing does not regret giving. Otherwise, how will the man with two tunics give one to the naked, unless he is the same man who can offer his cloak to the one who takes his tunic (Luke 6:29-30)? How will we make friends with money if we love it so much we cannot bear to lose it? We will perish with what is lost. What do we find here, where we have something to lose? It is Gentile behavior to meet every loss with impatience, since they probably put money before the soul. They do this when, driven by greed for gain, they undertake dangerous commercial risks at sea; when, for money's sake, they do not hesitate to face nothing in the courts that damnation should make them fear; when they hire themselves out for the arena and the camp, when they plunder on the roads like beasts. But we, distinct from them as we are, must not lay down our souls for money, but lay down money for our souls—whether spontaneously in giving or patiently in losing.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A is a faithful literal translation, and Pass B is a fluent rendering that correctly incorporates the required inline scripture citations (Luke 12:33 and Luke 6:29-30) which correspond to the thematic content of the Latin clauses. All nuances regarding agency (the Spirit being shaken, the man's hand on his property) and modality (the doubt regarding the man's ability to give) are preserved.
